summary: Specifies the format, contents, and semantics of Domain Name Registration Data escrow deposits for a domain name registry, so a registry's data can be safely stored with a third party.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard way for a domain registry to keep a backup copy of its records with someone trustworthy, in case something goes wrong.

questions: xml vs csv domain escrow deposit
subtitle: A standard layout for the backup copy a domain registry hands to an escrow agent, in either XML or CSV form.

tldr.problem: A domain name registry must periodically give a third party enough data to resume operations if the registry fails, but without a common format every deposit would be different and hard to check.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9022 defines escrow objects for domains, hosts, contacts, registrars, IDN table references and non-domain names, plus header, policy and EPP parameter pseudo-objects, in an XML model and an equivalent CSV model.
tldr.outcome: A registry can choose the model that suits its systems, extend it through a profile, and an escrow agent can run the listed verification tests on each deposit. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9022 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 8909, the Registry Data Escrow Specification.

sections.title: What Registry Data Escrow Is For
sections.content:
Registry Data Escrow (RDE) is the process by which a registry periodically submits data deposits to a third party called an escrow agent. The deposits hold the minimum data a third party needs to resume operations if the registry cannot function and is unable or unwilling to facilitate an orderly transfer of service. The stated goal is higher resiliency of registration services for the benefit of Internet users.

The RFC notes that escrow is a requirement for generic top-level domains (it cites Specification 2 of the ICANN Base Registry Agreement), that some country code top-level domain managers also escrow data, and that a similar requirement exists for ICANN-accredited registrars.

This document builds on the Registry Data Escrow Specification in RFC 8909. That specification covers the escrow process; RFC 9022 supplies the standard set of objects for a domain name registry.
sections.plainLanguage: If a shop might burn down, you keep a copy of the customer list at a friend's house. Escrow is that friend's copy, and this document says how to write the list.

sections.title: The Escrowed Objects
sections.content:
The objects follow the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mappings that registries already use to manage their data:

  • Domain, based on the EPP domain name mapping in RFC 5731.
  • Host, based on the EPP host mapping in RFC 5732.
  • Contact, based on the EPP contact mapping in RFC 5733.
  • Registrar, the organization that sponsors domains, hosts and contacts in the registry.
  • NNDN ("NNDN's not domain name"), a lightweight domain-like object for names the registry keeps without storing them as domain objects, such as a list of reserved names.

Four pseudo-objects round out the set. The IDN table reference points to the IDN table and policy used for internationalized registrations. The EPP parameters object lists what the registry's EPP server supports. The header carries object counts at a point in time. The policy object says which optional elements are required for this registry's business model.

A domain name can exist as a domain object or as an NNDN object, but not both.
sections.plainLanguage: The spare copy has a page for each kind of thing: names, the computers that answer for them, the people who own them, and the shops that sell them. There is also a cover sheet that says how many of each there are.

sections.title: The XML Model and the CSV Model
sections.content:
RFC 9022 defines two models for depositing objects. The XML model puts all deposit information, metadata and data, in an XML document defined by XML schemas. Its elements use the rde prefix, for example rdeDomain. The CSV model uses XML only to describe the layout of separate comma-separated value files; its elements use the csv prefix, for example csvDomain.

A deposit MAY mix both models, but each object MUST be escrowed in only one model. The RFC does not recommend either model and calls them equivalent. A registry whose database can export CSV may find CSV easier, while one that reuses its EPP code may prefer XML.

In the CSV model, each CSV file is described by an rdeCsv:csv element with a name and an ordered list of fields. The optional sep attribute sets the separator, with a default of a comma. Fields can be marked isRequired, and files can declare their compression, encoding (default UTF-8) and a checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: You can write the spare copy as one big structured document (XML) or as a stack of spreadsheets (CSV) with a note saying what each column means. Both hold the same facts.

sections.title: Domain Records and CSV Parent-Child Files
sections.content:
An XML rdeDomain:domain element carries the data of an EPP domain info response plus transfer data, Registry Grace Period status and DNSSEC key data. It has a name (the A-label for IDNs), a roid assigned at creation, status values, registrant and contact identifiers, name servers, the sponsoring registrar in clID, and dates such as crDate and exDate. The crDate and exDate elements MUST be present if the domain has been allocated. A separate rdeDomain:delete element lists names that were deleted and purged.

The CSV model treats files as relational tables. A child file marks its link to the parent with parent="true" on a field. For example, domainContacts, domainStatuses and domainNameServers are child files of the domain file, linked through the domain name field.

The links drive cascading changes in Differential and Incremental Deposits. When a domain record is updated, all its child records MUST first be deleted and then set again from the child files. When it is deleted, the child records are deleted too.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a main list of names and side lists for each name's owners and helpers. If a name changes, you throw away its old side-list entries and write fresh ones.

sections.title: Common Conventions
sections.content:
Several rules apply across all objects:

  • Dates and times SHALL be UTC timestamps as in RFC 3339, with no offset.
  • Country names SHALL be two-character identifiers from ISO 3166-1.
  • Telephone numbers MUST begin with a plus sign, then a country code, then a dot, then the digits.
  • IP addresses MUST follow the text form of IPv4 (RFC 791) or IPv6 (RFC 5952).

CSV files can carry an integrity checksum. By default CRC32 is used, and SHA256 MAY be chosen through the cksumAlg attribute. Parties receiving deposits MUST support both. Other algorithms are negotiated out of band, as are the supported compression formats.

Some elements come in an internationalized form (int), limited to the 7-bit US-ASCII subset of UTF-8, and a localized form (loc), which may use unrestricted UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone writes dates the same way, phone numbers the same way and country names the same way, so the copy can be read by anyone. A little check number on each file shows whether it got damaged.

sections.title: Header, Policy, Profiles and IDN Variants
sections.content:
Exactly one rdeHeader:header object MUST be present in every deposit, whichever model is used. It names the repository being escrowed (a TLD, registrar, privacy and proxy provider, or reseller) and holds count elements that give the number of objects of each type at a point in time, called the Timeline Watermark. An optional contentTag describes the expected content.

At most one EPP parameters object may exist at a given watermark. It SHOULD be included if the registry supports EPP, and it lists supported versions, languages, object namespaces, extensions and the data collection policy.

Because registries have different business models, each registry defines a profile. A profile extends base objects through XML substitution groups, uses a policy object to mark optional elements as required (the RFC's example is registrant), adds new escrowed objects, and gives the XML schemas to third parties who validate deposits.

A registry may escrow IDN variants as domain objects or as NNDN objects, but a given variant not as both. Explicit representations take precedence over variants computed by an algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The cover sheet counts what is inside. Each registry also writes its own house rules saying which optional boxes it always fills in, and IDN lookalike names are kept in exactly one place.

sections.title: Escrow Agent Verification
sections.content:
A data escrow agent SHOULD run an extended verification process, starting by building a test dataset as described in Section 5.2 of RFC 8909. The RFC lists these minimum tests:

  • Validate the deposits against the definition agreed with the registry. For the XML model, the deposits MUST be validated with the XML schemas of the profile.
  • Count the objects and check the total against the header element for that watermark.
  • Check that all contact objects linked to domains are present, and likewise all registrar objects and IDN table references linked from other objects.
  • Check that no domain name exists as both a domain and an NNDN.
  • Check that elements listed as required in the policy are present.
  • If an EPP parameters object was escrowed before, check that one and only one is present.
  • Check that the Timeline Watermark is not in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The friend holding the copy checks it: is everything there, does the count on the cover sheet match, and does anything appear twice? A good check now means a working backup later.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC does not define how deposits are transmitted. It says only that the format is the minimum needed to rebuild a registry without help from the original registry. Deposits, or at least the whole deposit, will often be confidential, so parties SHOULD take precautions such as encrypting data at rest and in transit. Authentication credentials MUST NOT be escrowed.

The registry and the escrow agent MUST each authenticate the other before data moves, and they MUST use integrity checking to ensure the data is what the source intended. If TLS is used, the recommendations of BCP 195 MUST be implemented. Where elements hold URLs, HTTP over TLS is RECOMMENDED. The RFC also warns that places with internal redundancy can become inconsistent, with harmful consequences.

On privacy, the format may be used to escrow personal data. The escrow process is governed by a legal agreement between the parties, which must ensure that personal data receives the required protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The copy has private details, so it should travel in a locked box. Both sides prove who they are first, and passwords are never put in the box.
